author: Gregory of Nazianzus
addressee: A congregation assembled for the annual commemoration of the martyr Cyprian
occasion: Gregory returns from the countryside one day after the commemoration and delivers a delayed encomium to a congregation that especially venerates the martyr.
argument: Gregory opens by lamenting that he almost missed the commemoration, then praises the bond of love among Christians. He singles out Cyprian as the most admirable of martyrs, both because of his eloquence and because of his dramatic conversion. He recounts how Cyprian, once a demon-worshipper, sorcerer, and persecutor, was converted after a Christian virgin defeated a demon sent to seduce her; the demon then afflicted Cyprian himself, and he sought release through Christ. After his conversion Cyprian publicly burned his magical books, became a bishop, and during the Decian persecution encouraged martyrs by letter from exile. Finally he was beheaded, and his hidden body was later revealed by God through a revelation to a worthy woman for the common good. Gregory closes by urging the congregation to imitate Cyprian's virtues and to stand firm against the devil.

outline.move: Gregory laments nearly missing the commemoration and promises to repay the debt of praise.
He celebrates the mutual love between himself and the congregation and begins to praise martyrs generally.
He introduces Cyprian's former life as a demon-worshipper, sorcerer, and persecutor, and defends recalling it.
He tells how Cyprian fell in love with a Christian virgin and sent a demon to seduce her.
The virgin defeats the demon through prayer and fasting; the demon turns on Cyprian, who seeks release through Christ, burns his magic books, and becomes a Christian and bishop.
During the Decian persecution Cyprian is exiled but encourages martyrs by letter, teaching contempt for earthly goods.
Cyprian is beheaded; his body is hidden by a devout woman and later revealed by God through a revelation to another worthy woman for public veneration.
Gregory exhorts each group in the congregation to imitate Cyprian's virtues and closes with a prayer to the Trinity.

cast.name: Cyprian
cast.who: The martyr being praised; formerly a demon-worshipper, sorcerer, and persecutor, later bishop and martyr.

cast.name: The Virgin
cast.who: A noble Christian virgin whose purity defeats the demon sent by Cyprian and leads to his conversion.

cast.name: Mary
cast.who: The Virgin Mary, invoked by the virgin as a helper.

cast.name: Decius
cast.who: The Roman emperor who persecuted Christians and under whom Cyprian was martyred.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle, cited as an example of one who recalled his former persecution of the church.

cast.name: Matthew
cast.who: The apostle and former tax collector, cited as an example of a converted sinner.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The psalmist, quoted in praise of the virgin.

cast.name: Solomon
cast.who: The king, quoted in praise of the virgin.

cast.name: Susanna
cast.who: The biblical woman rescued from wicked elders, cited as an example of divine protection.

cast.name: Thecla
cast.who: The early Christian virgin rescued from a tyrant suitor, cited as an example of divine protection.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.who: The patriarch, cited as an example of God's providential guidance.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: The righteous man whom Satan sought to test.

cast.name: Saul
cast.who: The Israelite king, cited both as one who sought relief through David's music and as one afflicted by an evil spirit.

cast.name: Beliar
cast.who: A name for the devil, the enemy arrayed against Christ.

scripture: Gregory uses the Septuagint (LXX) and its Psalm numbering. In a modern translation, cite as LXX Psalm numbering and use standard English book names, noting where LXX numbering differs from the Hebrew.
uncertain: The exact date of delivery; it is not stated in the text.
The identity of the Cyprian praised; Gregory appears to conflate Cyprian of Carthage with the legendary Cyprian of Antioch, but the text itself does not clarify this.
The precise location of the congregation addressed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Gregory returns from the countryside one day after the commemoration and delivers a delayed encomium to a congregation that especially venerates the martyr.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐξ ἀγροῦ μετὰ μίαν τῆς μνείας ἡμέραν ἐπανήκοντος
_unresolved_facts.fix: Gregory returns from the countryside one day after the commemoration (μετὰ μίαν τῆς μνείας ἡμέραν), but the text does not explicitly state that the congregation 'especially venerates' the martyr more than others—rather, Gregory says they honor him with annual honors and festivals (ταῖς δι' ἔτους τιμῶντες ἐκεῖνον τιμαῖς τε καὶ πανηγύρεσι), which is standard commemoration practice.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyprian: formerly a demon-worshipper, sorcerer, and persecutor
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Δαιμόνων ἦν θεραπευτής... καὶ διώκτης πικρότατος... καὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ταράσσων τὴν ἡμε τέραν ὁδόν... ὅσον κα κὸν καὶ γοητεία τούτοις προστιθεμένη
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyprian was a 'therapeutist of demons' (δαιμόνων θεραπευτής)—a worshipper/servant of demons, not merely 'demon-worshipper'; he practiced sorcery (γοητεία) and was a bitter persecutor 'in word and deed' of the Christian way. The brief's phrasing is acceptable but slightly flattened.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Virgin: A noble Christian virgin whose purity defeats the demon sent by Cyprian and leads to his conversion.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Παρθένος τις ἦν τῶν εὐπατρίδων, καὶ κοσμίων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The virgin is described as 'of noble fathers and well-ordered/modest' (τῶν εὐπατρίδων, καὶ κοσμίων), but the text does not explicitly call her 'Christian' at first—her Christianity is implied by her invocation of Christ and the Virgin Mary. More importantly, the brief omits that she was 'very beautiful in appearance' (καὶ ἡ παρθένος καλὴ τῷ εἴδει σφόδρα), which is crucial to the narrative as the reason Cyprian was captivated.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["5"]: The virgin defeats the demon through prayer and fasting; the demon turns on Cyprian, who seeks release through Christ, burns his magic books, and becomes a Christian and bishop.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸ τῆς νηστείας καὶ χαμευνίας προβάλλεται φάρμακον... Πίστεως γὰρ ὁ πόθος πρόξενος γίνεται... μετατίθεται τὸν πόθον... Προτίθησι δημοσίᾳ τὰς γοητικὰς βίβλους... πυρὶ δαπανᾷ τὴν μακρὰν ἀπάτην... ἀφίσταται τῶν δαιμόνων, οἰκειοῦται Θεῷ... καὶ νεωκόρος... Εἶτα ποιμήν, καὶ ποιμένων ὁ κράτιστός τε καὶ δοκιμώτατος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline omits that Cyprian first became a temple-keeper/neokoros (νεωκόρος) after requesting to do so to 'philosophize in humility for the cleansing of his former arrogance'—this is a significant step in his progression before becoming bishop. The brief jumps from 'Christian and bishop' without noting the neokoros stage.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["7"]: Cyprian is beheaded; his body is hidden by a devout woman and later revealed by God through a revelation to another worthy woman for public veneration.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸ σῶμα δὲ ἀφανὲς ἦν, καὶ ὁ θησαυρὸς παρά τινι γυναίῳ τῶν θερμῶν εἰς εὐσέβειαν... δημοσιεύει τὸ σῶμα δι' ἀποκαλύψεως, καὶ ταύτην γυναίῳ τινὶ τῶν ἀξίων τὴν τιμὴν καταθέμενος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The body was hidden by 'a certain woman of those zealous for piety' (παρά τινι γυναίῳ τῶν θερμῶν εἰς εὐσέβειαν), but the revelation was given to 'another worthy woman' (γυναίῳ τινὶ τῶν ἀξίων)—the brief correctly notes two women, but the text does not explicitly say the first woman 'hid' the body intentionally; rather the body was 'invisible/hidden' (ἀφανὲς) with her. The revelation was 'through a revelation' (δι' ἀποκαλύψεως) with God 'entrusting this honor to a worthy woman'—the brief's 'for public veneration' is implied but not explicit.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Christ (quoted): Introduced as 'that great voice' (τῆς μεγάλης ἐκείνης φωνῆς); the quotation is from Matthew 25:34
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τῆς μεγάλης ἐκείνης ἀκοῦσαι φωνῆς· Δεῦτε, οἱ εὐλογημένοι τοῦ Πατρός μου, κληρονομήσατε τὴν ἐπηγγελμένην ὑμῖν βασιλείαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says 'that great voice' (τῆς μεγάλης ἐκείνης φωνῆς), not 'that great voice' as a specific title for Christ—the phrase describes the voice they will hear, not necessarily marking Christ as speaker in a special way. The quotation is indeed Matthew 25:34, but the 'how_marked' should note it's presented as the eschatological voice of judgment, not specifically introduced as Christ speaking.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Job: The righteous man whom Satan sought to test.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ μέσος ἀγγέλων ἵσταται τὸν Ἰὼβ ἐξαιτήσων
_unresolved_facts.fix: Job is mentioned as the one whom Satan 'demanded to have' (ἐξαιτήσων) standing among angels, but the brief's description 'whom Satan sought to test' adds interpretive detail not explicit in Gregory's text—Gregory says Satan 'demanded' him, not specifically 'sought to test' him, though this is biblical context.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Saul: The Israelite king, cited both as one who sought relief through David's music and as one afflicted by an evil spirit.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὥσπερ Σαοὺλ ἐπὶ τὴν κινύραν τοῦ Δαβὶδ καὶ τὰ κρούσματα... συμπνίγων, ὥσπερ τινὰ Σαοὺλ δεύτερον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Saul is cited in two contexts: (1) seeking relief through David's lyre (section 5), and (2) as one 'throttled' by the demon, 'like a second Saul' (section 4). However, the second reference is to Saul being afflicted by the evil spirit that turned on him, not Saul seeking relief—the demon 'turns back against the one who threw it, throttling him like a second Saul.' The brief conflates these two distinct Saul references.
